en: Then, the practitioner of the Cakreśa-yoga, having offered oblations in the directions of the lotus pond and so forth, and having contemplated the water as having become empty, should visualize the *samayasattva* below the navel in the form of a serpent: [Vajravaruṇa], white in color, with a human face and seven hoods, embraced by his consort who holds a noose of snakes in her left hand, absorbed in union with Vairocana produced from the syllable *Bhrūṃ jaḥ cakra Bhrūṃ*, gracefully holding a blue lotus in his right hand, and possessing the form of a snake from the navel downwards.

Having summoned Vairocana by means of rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, and having caused him to enter after first offering the water for the feet (*argha*) and other honors, one should say, "Oṃ, you are the Vajra-samaya," and then consecrate him. Having worshipped him with flowers and so forth, one should cause the waves—which have been transformed into that [water], which possess reflections, consist of the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), and are endowed with the eight qualities because they are fragrant, sweet, light, clear, soft, cool, and do not harm the throat or stomach—to embrace the entire subterranean realm (*ārasātala*) as far as the abode of the eight families of *nāgas*.

If the patron has the capacity, one should construct a mandala centered on Vairocana by the water's edge; then, possessing the yoga of the Lord of the Wheel, one should offer a *bali* in the direction of the pond and so forth, and visualize that the water has become empty.

From *bhrūṃ* arises a wheel, and from *bhrūṃ* Vairocana is perfected; through his union with Locanā, he completely transforms into white Vajrāpāṇi, who has a human face and seven hoods. With his left hand holding a nāga-noose, he embraces and is in union with Śobhā.
With the right hand in the *g-yas pa 'gying ba* (the proud or haughty) gesture, one holds a blue lotus.

Having visualized the Samayasattva in the form of a nāga emerging from below the navel, one invites Vairocana by means of light rays from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart; preceded by the offering of the water for the feet (*argha*) and so forth, one causes him to enter by reciting: *oṃ vajrasamayas tvam*.

Having perfectly worshipped with flowers and other offerings during the manifest empowerment, and being endowed with the reflected image (*pratibimba*) resulting from that transformation, [he receives] the water of great sovereignty at the base of the throne—possessing the eight qualities: the nature of the nectar of primordial wisdom (*jñānāmṛta*), fragrant, sweet-tasting, light, stainless, soft, cool, and not harmful to the throat or stomach.
One should meditate everywhere upon it as being ultimately endowed with the abodes of the eight classes of nāgas and garlands of waves.

And there, upon the surface of the water, one should instantly establish the eight nāgas of the form to be described, fashioned as *samayasattvas* and non-different from the *jñānasattvas* summoned by rays of light from the seed-syllable in the heart.

Furthermore, within the center of the water, one should place the eight *nāgas*—whose forms will be described—having instantaneously transformed them into the form of the *samayasattva*. These, being inseparable from the *jñānasattva* summoned by the light rays of the seed-syllable at the heart, should be installed.
And therein:
*Karmādhikāravidhāna / Ācāryakriyā*, Chapter 9.
In groves of kumuda, utpala, and kamala lotuses,
and in lotus ponds, oblong pools, lakes, and the like,
[the fragrance rises] twice as high as the depth of their basins.
A circular piece of wood representing Varuṇa.
Furthermore, in ponds, flowing streams, wells,

and the like that are endowed with *kumuda*, *utpala*, and *padma* lotuses, one should plant trees whose nature is that of water-deities, arranged in a circle at a depth that is double [the height of the water].
One should place the great sacrificial post, its top marked with seven hoods, in the midst of the water,
and [worship] the nāgas in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should cause nine hooded serpents to be fashioned in sequence.

One should visualize [the tree] possessing a tip marked with seven hoods; it should be placed in the middle of the water, being a great tree. Furthermore, in the cardinal and intermediate directions are the nāgas, nine-hooded in succession.
In the center, due to the absence of a sacrificial post,
[he saw] Varuṇa, the king, well-fashioned from crystal;
his color was as white as that water.
Sweet-tasting, cool, and clear.

In the absence of the substance of wood, in the center, from crystal, there is the well-fashioned king of the water-deities; its water is white in color, fragrant, endowed with a delicious taste, cool, and stainless.
Outside of that, in the east, is Ananta, golden in color, with a head marked by a lotus;
its waters have the hue of crushed collyrium, are pungent and bitter, and are as terrifying as poison.

Outside of that, to the east, is a sign consisting of a lotus made of infinite gold, marked on its crown; its water is the color of powdered collyrium, bitter, pungent, and like poison—terrible to behold.
To the south is a lotus made of quartz, its head marked with the *śrīvatsa* symbol;
its water resembles jasmine, the moon, and a lotus stalk, and it is sweet.

The lotus, whose color is sweet and bitter and whose nature is like that of the southern mountain, possesses upon its crown the auspicious mark of a glorious calf; its water is like the *kunda* flower, the moon, and the lotus root—sweet and yet also bitter.
To the west is the terrifying Takṣaka,
whose head is marked with a *nandyāvarta* and made of copper;
his water resembles saffron and possesses astringent, pungent, and bitter tastes.
In the west is a terrifying pool made of copper, possessing a *śrīvatsa* on its surface; its water is like saffron, and it is extremely bitter, hot, and pungent.

In the direction of the Lord of Wealth (the North), one should visualize the water belonging to Vāsuki, the sovereign of the nāgas, whose hood is marked with a blue lotus fashioned of silver; its color is pungent, bitter, green, and yellow.
In the direction of Vaiśravaṇa, there is the lord of nāgas, Vāsuki, emanated from silver; upon the crown of his head is a blue *utpala* flower. His waters are green, yellow, hot, and cold.
In the northeast is the Great Lotus (Mahāpadma), its head fashioned of various colors and marked with a trident;
its water is golden-hued, waveless, sweet, pungent, and warm.
In the northeast is a great lotus made of white *jātya* [jasmine], marked with three points at its summit; its water has the luster of gold, is free of waves, and is fragrant, warm, and hot.
In the southeast (vaiśvānara), there is the lord of nāgas, Śaṅkhapāla, marked with a svastika;
his water is like saffron and turmeric infused with sweet and astringent flavors.

In my direction, from a dark blue *zha nye* [pigment], there arises the Lord of Nagas, Śaṅkhapāla, whose crown is marked with auspicious signs; his water is like saffron and cardamom, red in color, having a bitter taste, and providing satisfaction.
In the southwest is the lord of serpents Karkoṭaka, fashioned from bell-metal, with a neck marked by three rising lines;
his water is white, sweet, cool, and delightful.

In the direction of Nairṛta, there is a lake with very cool waves made of crystal; the nāga lord Balahaka has his neck marked with three upward-pointing lines, and its waters are white, sweet, cool, and delightful.
In the direction of the wind (the northwest), there is the Great Kulika, fashioned from iron, marked by a crescent moon upon his throat;
he is red and yellow in color, and his taste is sweet, astringent, and cool, and he is clear.

In the direction of the wind, there is the great Kulika, manifested from iron; his throat is marked by the phases of the moon. His water is red and yellow in color, sweet in taste, astringent, cool, and stainless.
The abode of the Nāgas' clans is to be inferred from the variations in the color of their water and the specific differences in its taste, for the successful accomplishment of all purposes.

Water is to be known through inference from the distinctions of its color, as well as the specific differences of its taste; furthermore, it brings about the successful accomplishment of all purposes for the various lineages and abodes of the nāgas.

Or rather, is it by reason that the lords of the nāgas have the right to dwell upon the surface of the earth as they please? For Ananta has gone to the fields and the ponds, while Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas, resides in the temple of the gods.

Furthermore, regarding those who exercise power over places such as plains and the like, speak according to the wishes of the lords of the nāgas. In the fields, there are infinite [nāgas] dwelling at the springs; in the abodes of the gods, there is the nāga king Vāsuki.
In the Buddha’s abode, Nanda and Upananda reside in the lotus ponds and lakes;
Śaṅkhapāla is on the peak of the mountain, and Karkoṭaka is on its ridges; they dwell in the water-channels and in the long lakes of the ocean.

In the ponds and pools of the Buddha’s abode, Nanda and Upananda sported in the waters of the streams; Śaṅkhapāla dwelt upon mountain peaks and in mountain valleys, while Baladeva moved through the oceans and rivers.

On the island, in the regions of rivers, ponds, and the earth, Takṣaka, the lord of nāgas, dwells in a delightful grove; and in a lake within a charming section of a garden during a flower festival, Kālika, the king of nāgas, resides.

Established upon the land of the *laṅkā* river in the continent, dwelling in the delightful forest of Kṛtavana, the sovereign of the Aja family; with the joy of blooming flowers in the groves and the black Nāgarāja in the various lakes and oceans.

In groves of lotuses, blue water-lilies, and the like, he should be known as Mahāpadma; in a cluster of great lotuses, as Kulika; and in a well or a reservoir, as Sāmānya—there is a distinction based on the quality of the water.

One should know that the Great Lotus resides in the stalks of water-born flowers; the noble Nāgas reside in wells and the waters within them; the excellence of the taste of the waters in equal springs resides there; and the Nāga Kings Padma and Utpala reside in forests and the like.
Having worshipped with streams of milk, clarified butter, sugar-candy, molasses, honey, mercury, and water,
one should perform the fire-oblation and other rites on the bank with dūrvā grass, kunda flowers, sesame seeds, and so forth.

One should offer perfect worship with milk, ghee, white substances, honey, and streams of quicksilver; likewise, one should perform fire offerings and other rites on the banks of rivers using *dūrvā* grass, *kunda* flowers, sesame seeds, and so forth.

The Great Master should offer the oblation with milk-rice mixed with the five nectars and honey, excluding the *madana* fruit; he should accomplish everything according to the ritual procedure of these mantras.

One should offer a *bali* consisting of the five nectars combined with honey, along with milk, ghee, and wine. Through the ritual procedure of the mantras of these [deities], the masters of the senses, infinite and truly exalted, [are propitiated].

Oṃ āḥ varuṇāya hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ anantāya hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ padmāya hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ takṣakāya hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ vāsukine hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ mahāpadmāya hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ śaṅkhapālāya hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ karkoṭakāya hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ kulikāya hūṃ svāhā | Having thus worshipped with white flowers using these heart mantras,

*Ku li k’a ya hūṃ svāhā*. These are the heart mantras. One should worship perfectly with white flowers.

With the left hand making the gesture of the hood (*phaṇābhinaya*) and the right hand in the boon-granting gesture (*varadābhinaya*), [he addresses] the deities: *Oṃ, Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Kulika, Varuṇapāla, Devati, Mahādevati, Soma, Śikhin, Mahāśikhi, Daṇḍadhara, Mahādaṇḍadhara, Apalāla, Huluhula, ...ndasāgara, Mahāsāgara, Anavatapta, Mahātaptā, Śrīkānti, Mahākānti, Surūpa, Mahāsurūpa, Bhadrāhi, Kamalodara, Śali, Mahāśali, come here!*
"Come, O great Nāgas! Bhūr bhuvaḥ hrūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Reciting this mantra for the Nāga bali offering, one should consecrate the milk bali.

With the left hand held in the gesture of support and the right extended in the gesture of supreme generosity, recite: *oṃ ānanta vāsuki takṣaka karkoṭaka padma mahāpadma śaṅkhapāla kulika varuṇapāla deveti mahādeveti somaśikha mahāśikhidaṇḍadhara mahādaṇḍadhara āpālala hulu hulu nanto pananta*.

Reciting the mantra for the *nāga* bali offering—*s'a ga ra ma h'a s'a ga ra aa na tapta ma h'a tapta | shr'i kanti ma h'a kanti | su r'u pa ma h'a su r'u pa | bha dra hi ka | ma ho da ra | si li ma h'a si li a'a gatstsha ta a'a gatstsha ta ma h'a n'a ga aa dhi pa ta ye bhu rbhu va h'uM phaT sv'a h'a*—one should consecrate the milk bali.

Thus ends the ritual procedure for the consecration of lotus ponds, tanks, wells, and so forth.
This is the ritual for the consecration of ponds, springs, and wells, performed so that young maidens may also be satisfied.
